report.verdict: A jackpot year, not a growth year. FY26 gross sales rose ~3% to NZ$1.67bn (~$0.95bn) on the record NZ$55m (~$31m) Must Be Won Powerball draw of November 2025 and three NZ$20m+ (~$11m+) jackpots, beating the original NZ$1,575.7m (~$898m) budget by ~6% but landing roughly NZ$15–25m (~$9–14m) short of management's own June-2026 forecast of NZ$1,693.2m (~$965m). Profit before distribution (company forecast NZ$401.4m / ~$229m; audited figure unverified) is flat-to-down on FY25's NZ$405.1m (~$231m) because prize cost, a 71% step-up in the problem-gambling levy, tripled ticket costs and halved interest income absorbed the volume — margin on sales down ~120bps to ~23.7%. FY27 hinges on the Powerball matrix change (10→14 balls) and the arrival of up to 15 licensed online casinos.

summary: **Headline: FY26 gross sales +3% to NZ$1.67bn (~$0.95bn).** Per Gaming Intelligence's coverage of the FY26 Integrated Report, sales (incl. GST) rose ~3% from FY25's NZ$1,626.9m (~$927m), i.e. ~NZ$1,676m (~$955m); that is still ~2% below the FY24 record of NZ$1,710.9m (~$975m) and reverses only part of FY25's 5% decline. The audited report itself could not be accessed — all FY26 full-year figures beyond the headline are management's June-2026 forecast or flagged as unverified.

**Beat the budget, missed the forecast.** The SPE FY26 budget (June 2025) assumed a 'normal' jackpot year at NZ$1,575.7m (~$898m) of sales; the June-2026 SPE FY27 raised the FY26 forecast to NZ$1,693.2m (~$965m) (+7.5%). The ~NZ$1.67–1.68bn actual implies a shortfall of NZ$15–25m (~$9–14m) against that forecast, all of it in H2: implied H2 sales ~NZ$767–772m (~$437–440m), roughly +1% on H2 FY25's NZ$762.2m (~$434m) versus the +3.6% management had pencilled in.

**Profit: company forecast NZ$401.4m (~$229m), -0.9% on FY25's NZ$405.1m (~$231m) — flat profit on +4% sales.** The original budget was NZ$360.8m (~$206m) with NZ$350.8m (~$200m) payable to the Lottery Grants Board (LGB) after a NZ$10m (~$5.7m) retention; the retention was dropped, so the full NZ$401.4m is distributable (+14.4% vs budgeted distribution). If H2 sales undershot by NZ$15–25m at a ~23–25% contribution, our estimate for audited FY26 profit is ~NZ$395–400m (~$225–228m) [estimate, unverified].

**Jackpots did the work — draw games 84.5% of sales.** The NZ$55m (~$31m) Must Be Won Powerball draw in November 2025 was the largest jackpot in Lotto NZ history; Powerball also reached ≥NZ$20m (~$11m) in August 2025, March 2026 and June 2026. H1 Lotto/Powerball/Strike sales rose 4.3% to NZ$763.6m (~$435m), +13.3% vs budget. Management's own SPE states that Powerball jackpot frequency and size is 'the single biggest driver' of any year's result.

**H1 FY26 (six months to 31 Dec 2025) was the strong half.** Sales NZ$903.4m (~$515m) +4.5% YoY / +12.0% vs budget; total revenue NZ$856.2m (~$488m) +3.9%; profit before LGB distribution NZ$227.4m (~$130m) +3.1% YoY and +20.8% vs the NZ$188.3m (~$107m) budget; operating cash flow NZ$278.0m (~$158m) +36%.

**Margin compression is structural, not just mix.** H1 gross profit rose only 0.9% on +4.5% sales (gross margin 31.8% of total revenue, -96bps); profit margin on gross sales 25.2% (-32bps); FY26F profit margin 23.7% vs 24.9% in FY25 (-120bps). Culprits: problem-gambling levy +77% H1 / +71% FY to NZ$5.5m (~$3.1m); ticket costs +131% H1 / +172% FY to NZ$15.2m (~$8.7m); prizes + prize-reserve contributions 54.1% of sales (+7bps); interest income -49% H1 / -53% FY to NZ$6.4m (~$3.6m) as cash is swept to the LGB and rates fall.

**Cost discipline is the offset management emphasises.** H1 opex NZ$45.2m (~$26m), -9.1% YoY and 13.1% below budget (5.0% of sales vs 5.8%); FY26F opex NZ$103.9m (~$59m) = 6.1% of sales vs 6.3% in FY25 and 6.8% budgeted. Part of this is mechanical: D&A fell 61% in H1 as the legacy gaming system rolled off amortisation after Project EDGE went live in September 2025. Employee remuneration still grew 8.0% (H1) / 8.6% (FY26F).

**Guidance bridge, FY26: budget NZ$360.8m → forecast NZ$401.4m (+NZ$40.6m / ~$23m).** Sales +NZ$117.5m (~$67m) vs budget contributed ~NZ$38m of gross profit; opex NZ$2.9m (~$1.7m) below budget added the rest. The division driving it is unambiguous — Powerball/draw games; Instant Kiwi retail (-2.1% vs budget), Keno (-2.1%) and Bullseye (-6.0%) all missed budget in H1, only Instant Kiwi Online (+26.7% vs budget) helped.

**FY27 budget: sales NZ$1,723.9m (~$983m), profit NZ$424.9m (~$242m), opex NZ$104.4m (~$60m, 6.0% of sales).** That is +1.8% sales / +5.9% profit on the FY26 forecast (≈+3% sales on the FY26 actual), premised on a 'normal' jackpot year plus the Powerball matrix change landing in H1 FY27. Prizes paid & payable rise to 51.1% of sales (from 50.0%) while prize-reserve contributions collapse to NZ$17.9m (~$10m) from NZ$64.7m (~$37m); retailer commission/MyLotto fees step up to 4.3% of sales.

**The strategic event: Powerball matrix change 10→14 Powerballs, announced March 2026, live H1 FY27.** Lower odds of a Division 1 win mean more frequent jackpotting, a new prize division and more weekly winners; Lotto and Strike are unchanged. This is the classic lottery 'odds change' playbook to re-engage infrequent players — it front-loads jackpot sequences but raises responsible-gambling scrutiny and makes the FY27 comp against the NZ$55m Must Be Won half even more jackpot-dependent.

**Regulatory overhang: up to 15 licensed online casinos from early CY2027.** They cannot offer lottery draw games (~84% of Lotto NZ sales) but will be able to offer instant-win and Keno-style products and to advertise across mainstream media. Management calls the FY27 financial impact non-material given the short window; we see the FY28+ risk concentrated in Instant Kiwi Online (H1 +25.9%, NZ$45.9m / ~$26m) and Keno (H1 -5.0%). All Lotto NZ games move to 18+ during FY27.

**Digital mix keeps grinding up.** 49% of H1 ticket sales came via MyLotto (48% in FY25); Instant Kiwi Online now 42.5% of Instant Kiwi sales (36.4% a year ago); MyLotto player funds on deposit NZ$17.4m (~$9.9m), +19% since June. Retail legacy products are shrinking: Instant Kiwi scratch -2.5%, Keno -5.0% in H1. Retailer commission plus MyLotto transaction fees held at 3.9% of sales.

**Technology programme: EDGE done, Frontier next.** Project EDGE (new core and interactive gaming systems) was delivered in September 2025 under budget — the most strategically important project in two decades per management — and no further profit retentions are required in FY26 or FY27. Project Frontier (new MyLotto website and apps) is targeted for first-phase delivery end-FY27/early-FY28; intangibles capex NZ$24.3m (~$14m) FY26F and NZ$21.7m (~$12m) FY27B, up from NZ$18.1m (~$10m) in FY25.

**Capital position: unlevered, cash-rich but cash-sweeping.** Zero borrowings (lease liabilities NZ$5.0m / ~$2.8m only); cash + term deposits NZ$261.7m (~$149m) at 31 Dec 2025, of which NZ$139.9m (~$80m) is restricted (unpaid prizes NZ$122.5m / ~$70m + player funds); unrestricted ~NZ$121.8m (~$69m). Equity peaked at NZ$131.6m (~$75m) at December and is forecast back to NZ$79.6m (~$45m) at June 2026 as H1 profit is paid out; FY26F cash payments to the LGB NZ$464.7m (~$265m), +9.5%, include the FY25 catch-up.

**Where every NZ$1 goes (FY25, confirmed by H1 FY26 ratios):** 54c prizes, 24–25c to the LGB, 12c taxes (GST, 5.5% lottery duty, problem-gambling levy), 6c operating costs, 4c retailer commission and MyLotto fees. Management's stated KPI is to hold community returns at ~25c per dollar — FY26F at 23.7c is below that bar.

**Five-year plan (SOI 2025–29): revenue NZ$1.82bn (~$1.04bn) and >NZ$400m (~$228m) of annual profit by FY29.** FY26 reached the profit marker two years early, but only because of jackpots — management's own 'normal year' profit was NZ$360.8m (~$206m). Sustaining >NZ$400m without abnormal jackpot runs is the real test, and it depends on the matrix change working.

**Governance and people.** Board Chair Mark Todd is listed as outgoing; Deputy Chair Kim Gordon signed the H1 accounts (20 April 2026) and the SPE with CEO Jason Delamore and Audit & Risk Chair Angela Dixon; CFO is Jeff Hayward. Chair succession lands in the same window as the matrix change, Frontier delivery and online-casino licensing. WLA Level 4 responsible-gambling recertification outcome due early FY27; Ministry of Health harm citations 0.7 per 10,000 players (FY25) vs <1.0 target.

**Management emphasis vs what's buried.** Emphasised: record jackpot, budget beat, costs 13% below forecast, EDGE under budget. Buried: profit below FY25 on higher sales, the H2 slowdown versus June forecast, the 71% levy increase and tripled ticket costs, declining Keno and retail scratch, and interest income shrinking to NZ$3.9m (~$2.2m) in FY27B from NZ$13.5m (~$7.7m) in FY25.

**Read-through for listed peers (The Lottery Corporation, Lottery.com-type digital, Scientific Games/IGT instant suppliers):** the NZ data confirm (i) jackpot dependency with a ~25% drop-through on incremental sales, (ii) digital at ~50% of lottery sales with instants migrating fastest, and (iii) online-casino liberalisation as the new competitive variable for instants and Keno. The matrix change is the same lever TLC pulled on Australian Powerball — watch whether NZ repeats that first-year uplift.

**Data gap, flagged explicitly:** the FY26 audited annual report was not retrievable (website is JS-rendered; article body paywalled). FY26 full-year profit, LGB transfer, product mix, full-year online share and year-end cash are shown as company forecast (SPE FY27, June 2026) or 'n/d', not as actuals.

segments.name: Draw games — Lotto, Powerball & Strike (~84% of sales)
segments.headline: Record NZ$55m Must Be Won draw powered a 4.3% H1 lift to NZ$763.6m (~$435m); H2 flattened as the jackpot cadence normalised, and FY27 now rests on the 10→14-ball Powerball matrix change.
narrative: They remain the monopoly provider of draw-based lottery in New Zealand and the Lotto/Powerball/Strike family generated NZ$763.6m (~$435m) of gross sales in the six months to 31 December 2025, up 4.3% YoY and 13.3% ahead of the NZ$674.0m (~$384m) budget, holding an 84.5% share of group sales (84.6% a year earlier, 84.1% for FY25 when the family did NZ$1,367.7m / ~$780m). The half contained the two events that made the year: a Powerball jackpot of NZ$20m-plus (~$11m+) in August 2025 and the NZ$55m (~$31m) Must Be Won draw in November 2025, which management describes as the largest jackpot in Lotto NZ history. Management is explicit that Powerball jackpot frequency and size is the single biggest driver of any year's result, and the half-year arithmetic bears that out — the entire budget beat is attributable to this line.

The prize economics moved against them modestly. Prizes paid and payable were 50.0% of group gross sales (49.8% a year earlier) and, with NZ$36.9m (~$21m) of prize-reserve contributions including interest transferred, the all-in prize cost was 54.1% of sales (+7bps). The prize reserve account balance rose NZ$22.2m (~$13m) over the half to NZ$87.6m (~$50m) and unpaid prizes climbed to NZ$122.5m (~$70m) from NZ$89.5m (~$51m) at June, consistent with large Division 1 prizes outstanding at period end; these balances are restricted cash and should not be read as surplus. Lottery duty at 5.5% of gross sales was NZ$49.7m (~$28m), and the problem-gambling levy jumped 77% to NZ$3.0m (~$1.7m), consistent with the new levy-rate period from 1 July 2025 [rate change itself not verified]. Promotion and retail support, the closest proxy for marketing, was NZ$10.6m (~$6.1m), 1.2% of sales (+7.0% YoY but 10.2% under budget) — jackpots advertise themselves.

The second half is where the story softened. The June-2026 SPE forecast implied H2 group sales of NZ$789.8m (~$450m), +3.6% on H2 FY25, helped by Powerball reaching NZ$20m-plus again in March and June 2026. The ~NZ$1.67–1.68bn full-year outcome implies H2 sales of only ~NZ$767–772m (~$437–440m), roughly +1% YoY, i.e. a NZ$15–25m (~$9–14m) miss against management's own forecast less than five months old. We cannot yet split the shortfall by game (product data for H2 is n/d), but given the 84% weighting and the fact that Instant Kiwi Online was running well ahead of budget, the draw family is the only plausible source. The lesson for FY27 modelling is that a NZ$20m jackpot in June does not carry the same sales elasticity as a Must Be Won in November.

Against that backdrop they are pulling the structural lever lotteries reach for when organic growth stalls: from H1 FY27 the Powerball pool expands from 10 to 14 balls (announced March 2026), lowering the odds of a Division 1 win so that the jackpot rolls more often and higher, with a new prize division and more weekly winners to keep participation broad; Lotto and Strike are untouched. The FY27 budget embeds this — group sales NZ$1,723.9m (~$983m), only +1.8% on the FY26 forecast but ~+3% on the FY26 actual, with prizes paid and payable rising to 51.1% of sales and prize-reserve contributions collapsing to NZ$17.9m (~$10m) from NZ$64.7m (~$37m), which tells you the reserve is already funded for the launch sequence. Our judgement is that the FY27 sales number is achievable if the change lands on time and the first big run arrives before Christmas, but the H1 FY27 comparison is against a half that contained a NZ$55m draw, so a YoY decline in H1 is a live possibility even with the change working. Responsible-gambling optics are the other cost: MoH harm citations were 0.7 per 10,000 players in FY25 (<1.0 target) and WLA Level 4 recertification is pending — a matrix change that lengthens jackpot runs will be watched by the regulator.

Regulation is otherwise benign for this family. The online-casino licensing regime arriving in early calendar 2027 (up to 15 operators) explicitly bars licensees from offering lottery draw games, and the move of all Lotto NZ products to an 18+ age limit in FY27 is expected to have a negligible revenue effect given how few under-18s buy draw tickets. The draw family is therefore protected product; the competitive exposure sits in instants and Keno.

segments.name: Instant Kiwi — retail scratch & Instant Kiwi Online (~12% of sales)
segments.headline: Instants +7.8% to NZ$107.9m (~$62m) in H1 entirely on digital (+25.9%); retail scratch -2.5%. Online instants are the product most exposed when licensed online casinos start advertising in early CY2027.
narrative: They sold NZ$107.9m (~$62m) of Instant Kiwi product in the half, +7.8% YoY and 8.4% ahead of budget, lifting the category's share of group sales to 11.9% from 11.6%. The composition is the point: retail scratch tickets fell 2.5% to NZ$62.1m (~$35m) (2.1% below budget) while Instant Kiwi Online rose 25.9% to NZ$45.9m (~$26m), 26.7% ahead of budget, taking the online share of instants to 42.5% from 36.4% a year earlier and 37.7% for FY25 (retail NZ$120.7m / ~$69m; online NZ$73.2m / ~$42m). Since Instant Kiwi is already an 18+ product, the FY27 age harmonisation changes nothing here; the growth is being driven by the MyLotto funnel, with player funds on deposit up 19% since June to NZ$17.4m (~$9.9m).

Cost-side, instants are the likely home of the ticket-cost inflation that shows up in group cost of sales: ticket costs rose 131% to NZ$6.6m (~$3.8m) in H1 and are forecast at NZ$15.2m (~$8.7m) for FY26 (+172%) and NZ$17.2m (~$9.8m) in FY27, versus NZ$5.6m (~$3.3m) in FY25. The filings do not break the line down by product; it plausibly also includes terminal ticket stock for the new EDGE retail estate, so we flag the attribution as unverified. Either way, at ~0.9% of sales it is now a visible drag on gross margin alongside the levy.

This is the segment where the regulatory change bites. Licensed online casinos — up to 15, with the first licences expected early in calendar 2027 — will be allowed to offer instant-win games and to advertise across mainstream media, something Lotto NZ has never had to compete against domestically. Management's position that the FY27 impact is non-material because of the short operating window is reasonable; our concern is FY28, by which time Instant Kiwi Online could be ~NZ$100m (~$57m) of annual sales growing 20%+ and squarely in the sights of operators with far higher payout ratios. Project Frontier (new MyLotto web and apps, first phase end-FY27/early-FY28) is the defensive investment, and its timing now looks tight relative to the competitive clock. The gross-margin profile of online instants versus retail scratch (no retailer commission, but MyLotto transaction fees and prize structures differ) is not disclosed — a gap we would press management on.

segments.name: Keno & Bullseye — daily numbers games (~3.5% of sales)
segments.headline: Combined NZ$31.8m (~$18m), -2.6% YoY and 3.0% below budget; Keno -5.0% is the weakest product in the portfolio and the one online casinos can replicate most directly.
narrative: They generated NZ$31.8m (~$18m) from the two daily games in H1, down 2.6% YoY and 3.0% below budget, with the category's share of group sales slipping to 3.5% from 3.8% (4.0% for FY25, when Keno did NZ$51.1m / ~$29m and Bullseye NZ$14.3m / ~$8.1m). Keno fell 5.0% to NZ$24.7m (~$14m) and missed budget by 2.1%; Bullseye grew 6.8% to NZ$7.1m (~$4.1m) but was 6.0% under budget, so management had expected more from both. Neither game benefits from jackpot cycles, which makes them the cleanest read on underlying player engagement — and that read is negative.

Strategically these are the products with the least protection. The SPE itself flags that incoming online-casino licensees will likely offer Keno-style games alongside instants, and will be able to advertise them. Management's product roadmap for FY27 is 'omnichannel enhancements' rather than a Keno relaunch, and with the entire innovation budget pointed at the Powerball matrix change and Project Frontier, we would not expect a turnaround here. At ~NZ$65m (~$37m) a year the category is too small to move the group, but a 5–10% annual decline is now the base case in our model and the FY27 budget of a 'normal year' implicitly assumes stabilisation that H1 did not deliver.

segments.name: Channels — MyLotto digital vs retail network
segments.headline: Digital reached 49% of ticket sales in H1 (48% FY25); EDGE refreshed the retail estate in September 2025, Frontier rebuilds the digital front-end by FY28; channel costs held at 3.9% of sales.
narrative: They put 49% of H1 ticket sales through MyLotto (web and app), up from 48% in the comparable FY25 period, with the balance through the retail network — so the digital crossover to a majority-online lottery is now a FY27–28 event rather than a distant one. Retailer commission plus MyLotto transaction fees were NZ$35.5m (~$20m), 3.9% of gross sales and flat as a ratio YoY, suggesting the mix shift toward online is not yet yielding a cost-to-serve benefit; the FY26 forecast has the line rising 10% to NZ$69.6m (~$40m), 4.1% of sales, and the FY27 budget steps it up again to NZ$74.0m (~$42m), 4.3%, which we read as retail incentives around the Powerball matrix launch. Retailer cost-recovery revenue (telecoms and terminal maintenance) is shrinking — NZ$2.5m (~$1.5m) in H1, -2.8%, and NZ$3.9m (~$2.2m) forecast for FY26 against NZ$4.9m (~$2.8m) in FY25 — as the EDGE rollout changed the terminal cost model.

Project EDGE, delivered in September 2025 under budget, replaced the core and interactive gaming systems and gave the retail estate a new terminal experience; the FY25 scorecard shows 100% availability across the retail network, core gaming system and MyLotto, with FY26–27 targets of 99.95%/99.97%/99.95%. Channel experience scores (share of customers rating 8–10) were 87% digital and 88% retail in FY25 against 80% targets, with FY26 forecasts of 86% and 85%. The 'digitally enabled players' metric — redefined in FY26 as MyLotto account holders — grew only 3.4% in FY25 against a +10% target that is retained for FY26 and FY27; this is the KPI to track once Frontier launches, because it is the closest proxy to active customers that Lotto NZ discloses (monthly actives and ARPU are not reported).

Project Frontier is the next capital cycle: new MyLotto website and apps, first phase targeted end-FY27/early-FY28, funded from the NZ$24.3m (~$14m) FY26F and NZ$21.7m (~$12m) FY27B intangibles capex with no profit retentions required. Intangible assets on the balance sheet rose to NZ$32.4m (~$18m) at December 2025 from NZ$27.6m (~$16m) at June. With licensed online casinos able to advertise from early 2027, the quality of the MyLotto experience becomes the moat for instants and Keno, so we regard any slippage in Frontier as a direct revenue risk rather than an IT footnote.

highlights.text: Sales +3% to NZ$1.67bn (~$0.95bn), ~6% above the NZ$1,575.7m (~$898m) budget, and H1 profit before distribution NZ$227.4m (~$130m) +20.8% vs budget — the record NZ$55m (~$31m) Must Be Won draw delivered exactly the kind of upside a lottery's option value promises.

Opex control is real: H1 opex -9.1% YoY and 13.1% under budget at 5.0% of sales; FY26F opex NZ$103.9m (~$59m) = 6.1% of sales vs 6.8% budgeted; FY27B 6.0%. Roughly half of the H1 saving is EDGE-related D&A roll-off (-61%), the rest is IT/gaming-system cost (-15%).
Digital engine: 49% of ticket sales online; Instant Kiwi Online +25.9% to NZ$45.9m (~$26m), 26.7% ahead of budget; MyLotto player funds +19% since June to NZ$17.4m (~$9.9m).

Project EDGE (new core + interactive gaming systems) delivered September 2025 under budget; no further profit retentions required in FY26 or FY27, so 100% of profit (NZ$401.4m / ~$229m forecast) flows to the Lottery Grants Board versus NZ$350.8m (~$200m) budgeted.

Balance sheet is debt-free: cash + term deposits NZ$261.7m (~$149m) at Dec-25, net cash NZ$256.7m (~$146m); operating cash flow +36% to NZ$278.0m (~$158m) in H1; FY26F operating cash flow NZ$405.2m (~$231m), +11.5%.

FY27 budget steps profit up 5.9% to NZ$424.9m (~$242m) on the Powerball 10→14-ball matrix change — the same odds-change playbook that has historically re-rated jackpot frequency for peers — with prize-reserve contributions already pre-funded (FY27B NZ$17.9m / ~$10m vs NZ$64.7m / ~$37m).

Responsible-gambling metrics remain best-in-class: MoH harm citations 0.7 per 10,000 players (FY25) vs <1.0 target; WLA Level 4 held since 2016 with recertification pending; Toitū net carbon zero maintained.

lowlights.text: Profit went backwards on higher sales: FY26F NZ$401.4m (~$229m) is -0.9% vs FY25's NZ$405.1m (~$231m) on +4.1% sales; profit margin -120bps to 23.7% of gross sales, below management's own ~25c-per-dollar community-return benchmark. Audited actual likely lower still (our est. NZ$395–400m / ~$225–228m) given the H2 sales shortfall.

H2 FY26 undershot the June forecast by ~NZ$15–25m (~$9–14m) of sales (implied H2 ~NZ$767–772m vs NZ$789.8m forecast, ~+1% YoY vs +3.6% planned) despite NZ$20m+ Powerball jackpots in March and June — jackpot elasticity is not linear, and the forecast was five months old.

Cost-of-sales inflation outside prizes: problem-gambling levy +71% to NZ$5.5m (~$3.1m) FY26F; ticket costs +172% to NZ$15.2m (~$8.7m) and rising again to NZ$17.2m (~$9.8m) in FY27B; retailer commission/MyLotto fees +10% to 4.1% of sales and 4.3% budgeted for FY27.

Interest income is evaporating as cash is swept to the LGB and rates fall: NZ$13.5m (~$7.7m) FY25 → NZ$6.4m (~$3.6m) FY26F → NZ$3.9m (~$2.2m) FY27B; cash + TDs forecast to fall from NZ$226.6m (~$129m) at Jun-25 to NZ$147.3m (~$84m) at Jun-26 and NZ$134.2m (~$77m) at Jun-27.

Licensed online casinos (up to 15) arrive early CY2027 with the right to advertise and to offer instant-win and Keno-style games — direct competition for Instant Kiwi Online (NZ$45.9m / ~$26m H1, +26%) and Keno (NZ$24.7m / ~$14m, -5%); Project Frontier's digital rebuild is not due until end-FY27/early-FY28.
Retail legacy products are in decline: Instant Kiwi scratch -2.5%, Keno -5.0%, and Bullseye 6.0% under budget in H1; the non-jackpot portfolio (~15% of sales) missed budget across the board.

Governance and disclosure: Chair Mark Todd is outgoing with the Deputy Chair signing the accounts during the matrix-change/Frontier/online-casino window; employee remuneration +8.0% H1 / +8.6% FY26F against a 1.1% total-opex rise; and the FY26 Integrated Report is not retrievable from the JS-only website, leaving full-year profit, LGB transfer and product mix unverified.

forecast.intro: Lotto NZ does not give market guidance; its budget (SPE, June 2025) and updated forecast (SPE FY27, June 2026) serve the same function. The FY26 bridge runs from a 'normal-year' budget of NZ$1,575.7m (~$898m) sales / NZ$360.8m (~$206m) profit / NZ$350.8m (~$200m) to the LGB, to a June-2026 forecast of NZ$1,693.2m (~$965m) / NZ$401.4m (~$229m) / NZ$401.4m — every dollar of the uplift from the draw-games division (Powerball: NZ$55m Must Be Won in Nov-25 plus three NZ$20m+ jackpots), with opex NZ$2.9m (~$1.7m) under budget and the NZ$10m (~$5.7m) retention dropped. The actual landed at ~NZ$1.67–1.68bn of sales (Gaming Intelligence), so the realised profit should sit slightly below the forecast [audited figure unverified]. For FY27 management budgets sales NZ$1,723.9m (~$983m), opex NZ$104.4m (~$60m, 6.0%) and profit NZ$424.9m (~$242m), +5.9% on the FY26 forecast, predicated on a normal jackpot year plus the Powerball matrix change in H1 FY27, a non-material impact from online casinos, no change to lottery duty (5.5%) or the levy, and no major system outages.

forecast.view: **Our FY26 close-out (estimate):** sales ~NZ$1,676m (~$955m), +3%; profit before distribution NZ$395–400m (~$225–228m), -1% to -2.5% YoY, margin ~23.6–23.9% of gross sales; full amount to the LGB; year-end cash + TDs ~NZ$140–150m (~$80–86m), no debt. **FY27 (year to June 2027):** we model sales of NZ$1.65–1.75bn (~$0.94–1.00bn) with a central case ~NZ$1.70bn (~$969m), i.e. +1–2% rather than the budgeted +3%, because H1 FY27 laps the NZ$55m Must Be Won half and the matrix change will not be live for the full period — a YoY decline in H1 FY27 (we pencil NZ$850–900m / ~$485–513m vs NZ$903.4m) is more likely than not unless the new odds trigger a NZ$40m+ run before Christmas. On a ~24% profit margin (prizes 51% of sales, GST ~5.9%, duty 5.5%, levy ~0.3%, commission ~4.3%, opex ~6.1%) that gives **profit of NZ$385–430m (~$219–245m), central ~NZ$410m (~$234m)** versus the NZ$424.9m budget; the matrix change is worth, on our arithmetic, roughly NZ$8–10m (~$5–6m) of profit for every 2% of incremental draw-game sales it generates. **Leverage** stays at zero; cash drifts down toward the budgeted NZ$134m (~$77m) at June 2027 as the balance sheet is run leaner, and interest income becomes immaterial. **Swing factors:** (1) jackpot sequencing — a single Must Be Won draw is worth ~NZ$10–15m of profit; (2) matrix-change go-live date and any regulator-driven delay; (3) first online-casino licence timing (early CY2027) and advertising intensity against Instant Kiwi Online/Keno — we haircut FY28 instants growth, not FY27; (4) levy and duty settings post the 2026 general election; (5) Frontier capex NZ$21.7m (~$12m) and delivery slippage. The thesis for LGB beneficiaries (Sport NZ, Creative NZ, NZ Film Commission, community grants) is that the >NZ$400m run-rate is now jackpot-and-matrix dependent rather than organically secured.
watch: Powerball 14-ball matrix go-live date in H1 FY27 and the size/duration of the first jackpot sequence — the entire FY27 budget uplift rests on it.
H1 FY27 results (due ~April 2027): sales vs the NZ$903.4m (~$515m) comp, opex vs the NZ$104.4m (~$60m) annual budget, problem-gambling levy and ticket-cost run-rates.
Timing of the first online-casino licences (expected early CY2027), their advertising launch and any sequential slowdown in Instant Kiwi Online (+25.9%) and Keno (-5.0%).
Release of the FY26 Integrated Report details: audited profit, LGB transfer, full-year online share, product mix and year-end cash — reconcile to the NZ$401.4m (~$229m) forecast.
Project Frontier milestones (first phase end-FY27/early-FY28) and intangibles capex vs NZ$21.7m (~$12m) budget; any further profit-retention request would signal overrun.
WLA Level 4 recertification outcome (early FY27), harm-citation trend post matrix change, and Board Chair succession.

Ticket-cost attribution to Instant Kiwi and the problem-gambling levy rate change are flagged as unverified. No earnings call exists (Crown entity). Share price reaction: not applicable (unlisted). report.sharePriceReaction: Not applicable — Lotto NZ (the New Zealand Lotteries Commission) is an autonomous Crown entity under the Gambling Act 2003 and Crown Entities Act 2004 with no listed equity or share capital; 100% of profit (less any Minister-approved retentions) is distributed to Te Puna Tahua / NZ Lottery Grants Board.
